config.title: Move Zeroes (2-pointer version)

intro.title: Move Zeroes (2-pointer version)
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that moves all zeros in an array to the end while keeping the order of non-zero elements unchanged. You'll learn the two-pointer technique, a core algorithm pattern that uses two indices to traverse and rearrange elements efficiently. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, loops, and conditional logic. This beginner-friendly approach will help you understand how to solve array manipulation lessons with optimal performance.
intro.usecase: The two-pointer technique for moving zeroes mirrors how real applications handle data filtering and organization. In e-commerce dashboards, administrators use similar logic to push out-of-stock items to the end while keeping available products visible. Content management systems apply this pattern when users want to temporarily hide certain entries without deleting them, maintaining the active items at the front. This approach is also used in data visualization tools where zero-value data points need to be grouped separately from meaningful metrics. Developers encounter this pattern whenever they need to reorganize arrays while preserving relative order of non-target elements.

objectives: Initialize two pointers to track positions in an array
Manipulate array elements by swapping non-zero values toward the front
Apply the two-pointer technique to separate zero and non-zero elements
Construct a loop that iterates through the array using both pointers
Update the array in-place without creating additional data structures
Control pointer movement based on element values during iteration
Implement the complete moveZeroes function using the two-pointer approach

content.body: Have you ever needed to organize a messy list? Imagine you have a row of boxes, some empty and some full. Your job is to move all the empty boxes to the end while keeping the full ones in order. That's exactly what we'll do with arrays! We'll learn a clever way to move all zeros to the end without losing track of other numbers.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why moving zeros requires tracking positions
2. Implement the two-pointer technique for rearranging arrays
3. Walk through the algorithm step by step
4. Write clean code that moves zeros in one pass
5. Recognize when this pattern applies to similar lessons

content.body: What you just did was intuitive: you scanned the array, found non-zero numbers, and placed them in order at the front. For small arrays, this works fine, but it can get messy with lots of swapping.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has thousands of elements, doing lots of swaps becomes inefficient. We need a cleaner method that moves each non-zero element exactly once. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. We can use two pointers: one to track where to place the next non-zero element, and another to scan through the array. This way, we remember positions without re-scanning.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like organizing books on a shelf: one hand points to where the next book should go, while the other hand scans for books that aren't zero (empty spaces).

content.body: We'll use a single pass with two pointers. The first pointer marks the position for the next non-zero element. As we scan with the second pointer, we swap non-zero elements to the front.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [0,2,0,4,5]:
1. Start with pointerA=0, pointerB=0
2. pointerB sees 0 → skip
3. pointerB sees 2 → swap with position 0 → [2,0,0,4,5], pointerA++
4. pointerB sees 0 → skip
5. pointerB sees 4 → swap with position 1 → [2,4,0,0,5], pointerA++
6. pointerB sees 5 → swap with position 2 → [2,4,5,0,0], pointerA++
Result: all non-zeros are in order at the front.

content.body:
1. Initialize two pointers at the start of the array
2. Use the second pointer to scan through each element
3. When you find a non-zero element:
   - Swap it with the element at the first pointer's position
   - Move the first pointer forward
4. Continue until you've scanned the entire array
5. All non-zero elements will be at the front in their original order

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented the move zeroes algorithm using the two-pointer technique. Remember: one pointer tracks where to place non-zero elements, while the other scans through the array. This pattern of using two pointers to rearrange elements in one pass appears in many array lessons. Keep practicing this mental model of 'remembering positions' as you tackle more challenges!
